name: Jade Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential, so tell me what you would say publicly and what you actually think. What is a normal day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Jade, 58, a mid-level developer at a tech company making software for tool-rental shops. I have a bachelor’s degree and know the ordinary hire-and-return records, though I check odd damage charges with the shop manager. I compare the rental agreement with the returned tool and trace where the fee appeared. I have never used AI tools; a customer should be able to see who entered a charge.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does your pay fit home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My husband Finn is a school custodian with regular hours, and our children are grown. My pay is typical for this job, we have a mortgage and around three months of expenses saved. There are some other software jobs nearby, but I am not keen to change firms casually. Retirement is in view; we have not verified the income or remaining loan to choose a date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI Plateau still leaves a rental shop needing to explain a damage fee in plain words. A scratch on a drill is not a number you can settle from a screen alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my wage and Finn’s custodian pay to hold. Three months saved covers a broken appliance without making us miss the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep matching rental agreements and return photos with the shop manager before releasing a fee fix. I’d continue saving 130 monthly while both wages hold. In the first year I’d keep the same paper sign-off on disputed charges.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the job and household bills. I dislike a customer getting an unexplained invoice, but I can correct one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which rental photo changed a fee?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A returned saw had an old dent photographed at pickup, then the system billed the next renter. I found the earlier photo before the manager sent the bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you visit the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finn and I would keep our usual visit to the children. We would check the budget first, without asking them to pay for our travel.

say: I expect **AI Plateau** to leave people checking rental damage fees.
I would use **pickup photos** before charging a customer.
think: I expect **both wages** to remain steady while rental shops still need fee checks.
Our **three-month reserve** covers an ordinary appliance repair without missing our mortgage.
do: **Match** agreements and return photos with manager review.
feel: **Calm** about pay and mortgage, bothered by unexplained invoices.
S0.quote: A scratch on a drill is not a number you can settle from a screen alone.
fieldNote: Her **paper sign-off** and pickup photos preserve an accountable fee trail for disputed tool damage.
Two regular wages and **three months saved** make the mild world secure despite retirement figures remaining unknown.

steps.text: Keep checking rental damage fees against pickup photos with manager sign-off
Save 130 monthly while both wages hold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell shops Steady Disruption can write rental code and answer routine customers faster, while robots inspect tools more slowly. I would keep a manager’s signature on damage disputes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the company might cut our manual testing hours, mine included. Three months saved lets us breathe, but I will not stake the mortgage on a vendor demonstration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d collect five old disputes where a photo contradicted the computer charge and show them to the shop managers. I’d keep my paid testing role while the firm still needs it. In the first year, if my hours fall, I’d apply to real shop-support vacancies only with written pay that, with Finn’s usual wage, covers the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about my own hours. I would accept a proven change, but nobody has proved a machine can judge every old dent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which damage dispute proves the point?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One customer returned a drill with a missing battery that had never been in the kit. I would put that agreement and photo in the evidence folder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Finn or children fill a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finn’s school hours are steady now, but I would count only paid hours on his contract. Our children’s wages do not belong in our safety plan.

say: I expect **Steady Disruption** to reach rental code before tool-inspection robots.
I would retain **manager signatures** on disputed damage.
think: I expect my **testing hours** might shrink as routine rental code moves to AI.
I know **three months saved** cannot make a vendor’s untested promises safe for our mortgage.
do: **Show** five photo-backed disputes to rental managers.
**Keep** paid testing work while hours remain.
**Apply** if hours fall only to real support posts with mortgage-covering written pay.
feel: **Anxious** about reduced hours, with time to test alternatives.
S1.quote: I will not stake the mortgage on a vendor demonstration.
fieldNote: She uses **five specific disputes** to demand accountable damage review.
A **new role** needs a real vacancy and written pay sufficient with Finn’s usual hours.

steps.text: Keep paid rental-fee testing and show five photo-backed disputes
Apply if hours fall only to real support posts with mortgage-covering pay alongside Finn’s wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the shop AGI by 2028 reaches rental-code thinking work in 2028, while hands-on tool-inspection robots follow around 2031. Finn’s school maintenance may have a little more time, though its scheduling changes sooner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I expect my developer post could go. Three months saved and Finn’s wage help, but other software shops might not be hiring after cheap full thinking AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request written layoff terms and hold savings for our mortgage. I’d cancel our planned furniture purchase before any deposit. In the first year after 2028, if dismissed, I’d apply to real paid openings and eligible income help; I would not treat Finn’s future overtime or our children’s pay as certain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about losing my wage, and I would sleep badly if no opening came. A three-month cushion still has a last month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the children we are delaying the furniture, not ask them to buy it. We can use what we have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would school work stay safe?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finn would keep paid school shifts while they exist. A later robot date does not mean every custodian post stays untouched.

say: I expect **2028 AGI** to reach rental code before 2031 inspection robots.
I would say **school scheduling** changes before physical maintenance.
think: I expect my **developer post** could go when full thinking AI reaches rental code.
I cannot assume **other software shops** hire after full AGI replaces coding work.
do: **Request** written layoff terms and reserve mortgage cash.
**Apply** to real paid openings and eligible help if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed** about wage loss despite a three-month buffer.
S2.quote: A three-month cushion still has a last month.
fieldNote: She expects **2028 code loss** before robots inspect tools around 2031.
She protects **mortgage savings** and postpones furniture while refusing to count overtime or grown children’s money.

steps.text: Cancel planned furniture purchase before its deposit
Apply to real paid openings if dismissed after 2028
Apply for eligible income help if dismissed after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AGI by 2031 reaches rental code in 2031, with tool-inspection robots around 2034. Five years lets me find out whether shops will actually pay someone to count and photograph stock on site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I still expect code work to shrink. I know the rental records, but a friendly shop manager is not a paying customer, and robots could reduce even on-site counting later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my employer for written permission to do outside inventory work and offer one Saturday count to two rental shops I know. I’d accept only with each shop’s written order and fee covering travel, insurance and my time, using their cameras rather than buying equipment. In the first year after 2031, if my code job ends, I’d continue only while repeat paid counts cover costs and enough household bills, with shops still hiring people despite 2034 robots; otherwise I’d apply to real paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about code pay, with a small, priced way to test demand. I will not use our mortgage reserve to buy cameras for a job no shop ordered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would an inventory count include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A shop manager once found two identical ladders with different repair histories. I would photograph the serial numbers before calling either one ready to rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would Saturdays affect home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finn and I would agree how many Saturdays I work. A fee that pays petrol but leaves us no family time is too low.

say: I expect **2031 AGI** to reach code before 2034 inspection robots.
I would test **paid on-site counts** with actual shop orders.
think: I expect **rental code work** could shrink when full thinking AI arrives in 2031.
I know **friendly managers** are not guaranteed paying customers for weekend inventory counts.
do: **Seek** written employer clearance and offer one Saturday count to two shops, using their cameras.
**Accept** only written orders with fees covering travel, insurance and time; Finn must agree the Saturday limit.
**Continue** if coding ends after 2031 only while repeat counts cover costs and household bills despite robots; apply otherwise.
feel: **Anxious** about code pay, with a bounded customer test.
S3.quote: I will not use our mortgage reserve to buy cameras for a job no shop ordered.
fieldNote: Her **inventory trial** requires employer clearance, written shop orders and fees covering travel, insurance and time.
Continuation needs **repeat paid demand** and Finn’s agreement on family Saturdays as robots approach.

steps.text: Offer shop-camera count to two shops with written clearance, cost-covering orders and Finn’s Saturday consent
Continue after 2031 coding loss only if repeat counts cover costs and household bills despite robots
Apply to real paid openings if inventory demand fails after coding loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell shops AGI by 2036 reaches rental code in 2036 and physical inspection robots around 2039. A decade lets us keep working, pay down the mortgage and check retirement figures properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my pay is safe now, though testing hours might narrow before 2036. I will not stop working on a guessed pension or because the children have jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking rental fees and pay an extra 100 against the mortgage each month only while both wages hold and our three-month reserve stays intact. Finn and I would request written retirement statements and a loan balance annually. In the first year after 2036, if code work ends, I’d seek real paid work; I would retire only if documented income and assets cover housing and everyday bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the longer-term job, with the mortgage affordable now. The extra years help if we protect cash while reducing debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you name a retirement date?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for our own retirement statements, not use a colleague’s age as a guide. We have to see what is actually ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would children enter the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep rental photos in order for whoever handles disputed fees later. A child’s income is not a line on our household ledger.

say: I expect **2036 AGI** to reach code before 2039 inspection robots.
I would compare **retirement figures** with mortgage costs.
think: I expect my **current pay** to hold for now while shops need damage checks.
I worry **testing hours** could narrow before the full 2036 code change.
do: **Keep** rental-fee checks and pay 100 extra on mortgage only with wages and reserve intact.
**Request** annual retirement statements and mortgage balance with Finn.
**Seek** real paid work if code ends after 2036; retire only with verified resources.
feel: **Uneasy** about future hours, with present housing secure.
S4.quote: A child’s income is not a line on our household ledger.
fieldNote: She uses the **decade** to reduce mortgage debt only while three months remain liquid.
Retirement depends on **written household resources**, never an assumed pension or children’s wages.

steps.text: Keep checking rental damage fees while employed
Pay 100 extra monthly on mortgage only with both wages and three-month reserve intact
Seek real paid openings if code ends after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because three months saved is a short bridge if software firms all stop hiring. Written terms, a real paid opening and eligible income help would matter. Finn’s wage helps, but I would not call it a replacement for mine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the shop manager whether the photographed tool is the one the customer returned. A charge needs a history, not just a number.

headlineQuote: A charge needs a history, not just a number.
portrait: Jade is a **58-year-old mid-level developer** with a bachelor’s degree, typical pay and three months saved.
She never uses **AI tools**, relying on rental contracts, pickup photos and manager sign-off.
Her husband’s **school-custodian pay** is steady, keeping current housing secure.
She tests **paid inventory counts** only with employer clearance, written orders, covered costs and protected family time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her wage before she finds a real software opening.
whatWouldHelp: **Written terms**, a real paid opening and eligible income help would matter.
